title: After 1997, lower river areas lost about the same runoff fraction as their headwaters at 35-40 nested south-east Australian gauge sets; stream loss between gauges was small (AGCD rain)
abstract: Question: after 1997, south-east Australian runoff fell 15-25% below its 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation and stayed low. Did streams lose this water to falling groundwater in channels and valley floors? This predicts a larger fractional loss in the lower part of a basin than in its headwaters. Approach: we used 35-46 nested CAMELS-AUS v2.03 gauge sets (a downstream gauge and its upstream gauges; mostly Victoria). For headwater, incremental (between-gauge) and whole downstream areas we fitted annual runoff on rain, prior-year rain and temperature in 1951-1996 and measured later residuals. A daily test compared downstream and lagged upstream flow on dry days. Results (AGCD rain, 2010-end): headwaters lost 15.5% (95% interval 9.7-21.6), incremental areas 18.1% (10.0-26.2); difference -2.6 points (-10.1 to +4.4), inconclusive by our pre-set rule. Whole downstream catchments lost the same fraction as their headwaters (-0.2 points, -4.0 to +3.3), so extra loss between gauges was at most about one quarter of the downstream deficit. Net-losing dry days rose 2.8 points (1.1-4.7) in 1997-2009, more in flat valleys, but this was about 2 mm/yr, against an annual deficit that grew to 37 mm/yr, and it weakened after 2010. With SILO rain the headwater deficit almost vanished (-1.2%) and the incremental-minus-headwater difference was -6.3 points (-16.1 to +1.6); AGCD rose against SILO more in headwaters (4.2%) than in incremental areas (2.5%). Conclusion: channel and valley-floor losses do not explain the persistent loss at this scale; a loss that acts on all parts of the catchments fits better. Limitations: small mostly upland sample, rain-product dependence, two-gauge errors, and no test of disconnection that is equal in all streams.
